title: Gaining Conviction for a Decision
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that acting decisively with limited information requires conviction, the earned certainty that turns a view into committed action. It distinguishes conviction from confidence, which is only a judgment about the odds, and from stubbornness, which no longer listens. Leaders can build conviction deliberately through four steps: frame the choice as several real options, name what would have to be true for each option to be right and test the weakest condition first, invite the strongest possible challenge, and articulate the view repeatedly to different audiences. The final step comes last because repetition builds certainty whether or not a view is right. Conviction built this way is not rigid, because the conditions that must hold become tripwires that signal when to revisit the decision. The note closes by saying the goal is decisions worth committing to, not never being wrong.
points: Conviction is earned certainty followed by a deliberate commitment, and it differs from both confidence and stubbornness.
Weigh several real options rather than a single yes-or-no proposal, since alternatives make decisions fail far less often.
Write down what would have to be true for each option to be right and test the weakest condition first.
Seek the best argument against your view; a view that survives a strong challenge is held more firmly.
Repeat and state the view publicly only after it has passed the earlier tests, and keep the underlying conditions as tripwires.
quotes: Conviction is not the same as confidence, which is only a judgment about the odds of being right. Nor is it stubbornness, which is certainty that no longer listens.
Conviction is certainty that has been earned, followed by a deliberate choice to commit.

Considering several real options, rather than debating a single proposal, is essential. Paul Nutt’s studies found that organizational decisions framed as yes or no failed far more often than those weighed as alternatives. Options give conviction the soil from which to grow.
Leaders write these conditions down and then test the weakest of them first, because that is where a view is most likely to break.
Leaders who hold firm against a strong competing argument become more certain of their view.
Repetition builds certainty whether or not a view is right, so it should strengthen only views that have already passed the earlier tests.

Because leaders know what would have to be true for their decision to be right, they also know what evidence would tell them to revisit it. That evidence becomes a set of tripwires, which let leaders commit fully now while staying alert to signals that matter.
The ultimate goal is not to be a leader who is never wrong, but one whose decisions are worth committing to.
